In [[geometry]], the '''dual snub 24-cell''' is a 144 vertex convex [[4-polytope]] composed of 96 irregular [[cell (mathematics)|cells]]. Each cell has faces of two kinds: three [[Kite (geometry)|kites]] and six isosceles triangles. The polytope has a total of 432 faces (144 kites and 288 isosceles triangles) and 480 edges.

== Geometry ==
The [[snub 24-cell]] is a convex uniform [[4-polytope]] that consists of 120 [[Regular tetrahedron|regular tetrahedra]] and 96 [[Regular icosahedron|icosahedra]] as its [[Cell (geometry)|cell]], firstly described by [[Thorold Gosset]] in 1900.{{sfn|Gosset|1900}} Its dual is a semiregular,{{sfn|Coxeter|1973|pp=151-153|loc=§8.4. The snub {3,4,3} }} first described by {{harvtxt|Koca|Al-Ajmi|Ozdes Koca|2011}}.{{sfn|Koca|Al-Ajmi|Ozdes Koca|2011}} 

The vertices of a dual snub 24-cell are obtained using [[quaternion]] simple roots <math>T'</math> in the generation of the 600 vertices of the [[120-cell]]. The following describe <math>T</math> and <math>T'</math> [[24-cell]]s as quaternion orbit weights of <math>D_4</math> under the [[Weyl group]] <math>W(D_4)</math>:{{sfn|Koca|Al-Ajmi|Ozdes Koca|2011|loc=6. Dual of the snub 24-cell|pp=986-988}}<math display="block">\begin{align}
 O(0100)&: T = \left\{\pm 1,\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3,\frac{\pm 1 \pm e_1 \pm e_2 \pm e_3}{2}\right\} \\
 O(1000)&: V_1 \\
 O(0010)&: V_2 \\
 O(0001)&: V_3 \\
T' &= \sqrt{2} (V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus V_3) = \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{-1 - e_1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1 - e_1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-1 + e_1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1 + e_1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-e_2 - e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{e_2 - e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-e_2 + e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{e_2 + e_3}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\frac{-1 - e_2}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1 - e_2}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-1 + e_2}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1 + e_2}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-e_1 - e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{e_1 - e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-e_1 + e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{e_1 + e_3}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\frac{-e_1 - e_2}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{e_1 - e_2}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-e_1 + e_2}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{e_2 + e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-1 - e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1 - e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{-1 + e_3}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1 + e_3}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}</math>

With quaternions <math>(p,q)</math> where <math>\bar p</math> is the conjugate of <math>p</math> and <math>[p,q]:r\rightarrow r'=prq</math> and <math>[p,q]^*:r\rightarrow r''=p\bar rq</math>, then the [[Coxeter group]] <math>W(H_4)=\lbrace[p,\bar p] \oplus [p,\bar p]^*\rbrace </math> is the symmetry group of the [[600-cell]] and the [[120-cell]] of order 14400.

Given <math>p \in T</math> such that <math>\bar p=\pm p^4</math>, <math>\bar p^2=\pm p^3</math>, <math> \bar p^3=\pm p^2</math>, <math>\bar p^4=\pm p</math> and <math>p^\dagger</math> as an exchange of <math>-1/\phi \leftrightarrow \phi</math> within <math>p</math>, where <math display="inline">\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}</math> is the [[golden ratio]], one can construct the snub 24-cell <math>S</math>, 600-cell <math>I</math>, 120-cell <math>J</math>, and alternate snub 24-cell <math>S'</math> in the following, respectively:<math display="block">\begin{align}
 S = \sum_{i=1}^4\oplus p^i T, &\qquad I=T+S=\sum_{i=0}^4\oplus p^i T, \\
J=\sum_{i,j=0}^4\oplus p^i\bar p^{\dagger j}T', &\qquad S'=\sum_{i=1}^4\oplus p^i\bar p^{\dagger i}T'.
\end{align}</math>This finally can define the dual snub 24-cell as the orbits of <math>T \oplus T' \oplus S'</math>.

== Cell ==
[[File:Cell of the dual snub 24-cell (transparent).svg|thumb|The cell of dual snub 24-cell]]
The dual snub 24-cell has 96 identical cells. The cell can be constructed by multiplying <math display=inline> \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} </math> to the eight Cartesian coordinates:
<math display=block> \begin{matrix} (-\phi, 0, 1), &\qquad (0, -1, -\phi), &\qquad (1, \phi, 0), \\
 (-\varphi, \varphi, -\varphi), &\qquad (\varphi, -\varphi, \varphi), &\qquad (\varphi^2, 0, 1), \\
 (1, -\varphi^2, 0), &\qquad (0, -1, \varphi^2),
\end{matrix}</math>
where <math display=inline> \phi = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} </math> and <math display=inline> \varphi = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2} </math>. These vertices form six [[isosceles triangle]]s and three [[kite (geometry)|kites]], where the legs and the base of an isosceles triangle are <math display=inline> \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} </math> and <math display=inline> \frac{\phi}{\sqrt{2}} </math>, and the two pairs of adjacent equal-length sides of a kite are <math display=inline> \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} </math> and <math display=inline> \frac{\varphi^2}{\sqrt{2}} </math>.{{sfn|Koca|Al-Ajmi|Ozdes Koca|2011|p=986&ndash;987}}
